video_title: Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is Running Out of Copper
gist: Ex-Nvidia photonics engineer Yannick and Teema co-founder Herwig argue copper is hitting limits in AI clusters, energy is the binding constraint, and photonics supply chain gaps (lasers, tools, substrates) create an opening for a European foundry targeting 2027 production.

themes.theme: Copper to optics in AI networks

insights.claim: AI models no longer fit on one GPU, so many GPUs must be linked; copper interconnects are running out of headroom as processors need more data at higher speeds, forcing a move to optical links with far higher bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: The interconnect, not just the compute, is the AI scaling bottleneck, which favors photonics suppliers.
insights.quote: copper is gradually exhausting its resources

insights.claim: Agentic AI makes the model call tools on other servers and return results to the GPU, creating heavy latency-sensitive east-west traffic; this pushes data centers toward flatter, much denser networks with many more direct switch-to-GPU connections than traditional deep switch trees.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: Flatter topologies multiply the number of links per GPU, increasing optical transceiver and laser demand per cluster.

insights.claim: Half of a modern AI factory is GPUs and the other half is the technology that connects them, which the speaker sees as a huge opportunity for optics and photonics.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Interconnect content per AI dollar is large and under-appreciated relative to GPU focus.
insights.quote: half of it is GPUs, and the other half is the technology to connect them

insights.claim: Data center CTOs say energy consumption is their number one worry, since CEOs demand growth but nobody can supply grid power; Google reportedly spent three years negotiating with Amsterdam and ended up moving plans to Belgium over grid access.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Grid access, not capital, gates data center siting and growth, so energy-efficient interconnect has real value.
insights.quote: Google spent three years negotiating with Amsterdam

insights.claim: Grid modernization or new power plants cannot arrive on the timeline data center buildouts require, so a more fundamental efficiency solution is needed; the speaker calls data center energy use the 'killer app' for photonics, a technology developed for 20-30 years on the science side.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Photonics adoption is pulled by an energy-efficiency need rather than pure bandwidth.
insights.quote: the energy consumption of data centers in the field of AI is the same killer application

insights.claim: The speaker contrasts US hostility toward data centers with Europe, where stricter regulation and a smaller data center base mean less aversion, and argues Europe could build a different, more energy-efficient non-hyperscaler data center network.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: European AI infrastructure could differentiate on efficiency, but this is aspirational.

themes.theme: Nvidia's photonics push and supply chain gaps

insights.claim: Nvidia escalated its photonics messaging from talk to action: louder in 2024, a market push in 2025, and in 2026 investments in Lumentum and Coherent that, in the first six months of the year, were reportedly four times the total market volume.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Nvidia is using its balance sheet to pre-build photonics supply, signalling that laser capacity is strategic.
insights.quote: In the first 6 months of this year, they invested four times more than the total market volume.

insights.claim: Lumentum and Coherent are the two leading Western laser makers and effectively the only ones with that capability at scale; the host noted Lumentum's shares rose roughly a thousandfold in a year and that its CEO is overwhelmed with demand.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Laser supply is concentrated in two Western names, giving them pricing power until new capacity arrives.

insights.claim: Foundries such as TSMC, GlobalFoundries and Tower have invested in silicon photonics wafers, but delivering a wafer is not what Nvidia ordered, which is a finished chip; the missing middle needs lasers, packaging and scaled manufacturing, and no industrial player occupies that middle layer.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Value may accrue to specialist back-end photonics manufacturers between wafer and finished module.

insights.claim: Photonics scale-up is constrained by inadequate tool throughput, poor yield and efficiency of finished products, scarce substrates with only a handful of suppliers, and an East-West split; tool makers are not building nearly enough equipment.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: Equipment and raw-material shortages cap photonics supply growth for the whole industry, not just startups.
insights.quote: Tool manufacturers are not building even close to enough tools.

insights.claim: Customer-requested photonics volumes exceed Teema's own very ambitious forecasts, so the limiting factor is delivery schedules rather than demand.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: Demand visibility for photonics capacity is strong; execution is the risk.

insights.claim: Early market forecasts were too low: the speakers cited Andy Bechtolsheim calling out numbers far above even the most optimistic analyst forecasts, which helped convince them to start Teema.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Insiders were more bullish on photonics volumes than sell-side models.

insights.claim: Teema bought a bankrupt large European plant in the 2023-24 period, about 20 km from IMEC, with permits, cleanrooms and infrastructure already in place; since a foundry of this size is normally a 3-5 year project, this shortcut gave a head start.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Distressed fab assets plus talent proximity let a startup compress the usual foundry timeline.

insights.claim: Teema plans to begin production in 2027 and reach full capacity by 2028.
insights.speaker: Yannick (ex-Nvidia, Teema)
insights.so_what: New European photonics capacity arrives only in 2027-28, so shortages likely persist until then.

insights.claim: The European Council's Chips Act II language reportedly prioritizes photonics, with a focus on industrialization and clean manufacturing, which the speaker says almost reads like a definition of Teema; sovereignty is a driver.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Policy support may subsidize European photonics capacity.

insights.claim: Between 2000 and 2015, about 4,000 peer-reviewed photonics papers were published worldwide and 35% came from Ghent University, evidence of Belgium's deep photonics research base.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: Europe's talent base in photonics is concentrated and a basis for the industrial pitch.

insights.claim: European photonics innovations have historically been commercialized in Taiwan or the US; the speaker invokes ASML as the precedent of a European 40-year deep-tech success and argues Europe is more ready than assumed, while US prospects questioned Teema on financing, talent, equipment and speed.
insights.speaker: Herwig (Teema co-founder)
insights.so_what: The bull case on European deep tech rests on a precedent, not yet proof.
insights.quote: Europe has already done it once
